result.white_space: The Phase 1 software (per-tender snapshot, hash or seal, override log, discovery export) is already sold by at least DOTScreener ($99/mo) and Cipher & Row ($149-$449/mo, with Ed25519 and RFC 3161). SaferWatch, Descartes AuditLog and Highway Load Lock each cover part of it. Selling it at $299/month with a 'Discovery Fire Drill' would be a price and feature race against products that are cheaper and already marketed on the same Montgomery deposition angle. Three narrow pieces look unserved, though I could not confirm that none exists. (1) Insurance-linked use of the data: I found no vendor that turns tender-level vetting data into a placed contingent-auto or broker-liability program with a documented premium credit for small brokers ($2M-$60M gross revenue). Marsh BrokerSafe is large-broker and analytics-based, and RPS says capacity is tightening. Underwriters and wholesalers say they want vetting evidence but publish no way to submit it. (2) Override discipline as an underwriting signal: no competitor sells 'who overrode which failed check, when and why' as a scored, benchmarked metric that underwriters can rate. Most only log it. (3) A counsel-authored written carrier-selection standard with per-rule pass/fail evidence. Competitors record 'what was checked', while the idea's 'which of the broker's own written rules the carrier passed' is more specific. I found no vendor bundling defense-counsel-drafted standards. TMS-agnostic ingestion via CSV or rate-con email forwarding is a small integration edge, but Highway already integrates with McLeod, Turvo, Revenova and Tai. Caveat: DOTScreener and Cipher & Row disclose no funding, founders or customer counts, so they may be thin, but a low-price entrant can copy the unserved pieces quickly.
result.evidence_of_demand: Demand for the problem is strong. Demand for a stand-alone snapshot SaaS at $299/month is weak because cheaper products exist. Evidence: (1) RPS says Montgomery is creating a capacity issue for broker contingent liability (https://www.theinsurer.com/e-and-s/news/montgomery-ruling-creating-capacity-issue-for-freight-broker-contingent-2026-09-17/). The Insurer's Sept 24 piece says insurers are pushing broker exposure into the specialty market after a 'paradigm shift' (https://www.theinsurer.com/ti/news/insurers-push-freight-broker-exposure-into-specialty-market-after-paradigm-shift-2026-09-24/); I could only read that from search snippets. (2) Specialty Program Group says underwriters must now assess broker carrier-selection practices and vetting protocols, and brokers that can demonstrate rigorous vetting will get the most competitive pricing (https://www.specialtyprogramgroup.com/blog/underwriting-transportation/montgomery-v-caribe-transport-the-insurance-industry-needs-to-pay-attention/). (3) FreightWaves says documented, data-driven vetting will earn better rates and that contingent auto may become mandatory across about 28,000 brokerages (https://www.freightwaves.com/news/the-freight-broker-insurance-gap-is-now-real). (4) Vendors are spending on it: Descartes shipped AuditLog within six weeks of the ruling (https://www.stocktitan.net/news/DSGX/new-audit-log-capability-from-descartes-helps-organizations-create-grq09sy5c1cy.html), Highway mandated ELD hookups (https://www.freightwaves.com/news/highway-post-montgomery-requiring-eld-hookups-for-all-carriers), and a cluster of law-firm and vendor guides say to keep per-load records (https://www.brokerpro.com/posts/montgomery-caribe-carrier-vetting/, https://transfix.io/insights/carrier-vetting-after-montgomery-v-caribe-what-broker-compliance-now-requires). (5) TIA is lobbying FMCSA for a federal carrier-selection standard and a 'high risk' list (https://www.ttnews.com/articles/montgomery-ruling-unknowns), and Lockton notes the Court did not define reasonable scrutiny (https://global.lockton.com/us/en/news-insights/the-supreme-courts-montgomery-ruling-raises-the-stakes-for-freight-brokers), which raises demand for defensible written standards. Price anchors: DOTScreener $99, CarrierOk $149-$499, Cipher & Row $149-$449, Descartes MyCarrierPortal about $515+. No forum complaints from small brokers about lacking tender-time proof were found, and Reddit or Facebook-group evidence was not retrievable.
result.sharper_angle: Do not build the snapshot-logger SaaS as the product. DOTScreener, Cipher & Row, SaferWatch, Descartes and Highway already cover it, mostly at lower prices. Treat the snapshot as a free or near-free data feed and make the business an insurance-distribution play for small brokers: 'the broker liability program that prices your tender-time discipline.' (1) Get a wholesaler or MGA (RPS, Falvey, Reliance Partners and Loadsure are candidates; Marsh BrokerSafe is the large-broker benchmark) to agree first to a filed premium credit or an easier underwriting path for brokers who pass an evidence standard. Sign that partner before writing software. (2) Define the evidence standard: counsel-drafted written carrier-selection rules, per-tender pass/fail against those rules, an override rate and override-approver metric, and an independently verifiable sealed record. Accept the record from any source, whether your logger or DOTScreener, Cipher & Row, Highway or SaferWatch, so you are the underwriting-evidence layer and not another vetting tool. (3) Earn commission on placed premium (10-15%), with the software as a lead-generation and retention tool. (4) Validate in the first 30 days by getting two wholesalers to state in writing what credit or capacity they would give. If none will, the Phase 2 thesis fails, and the fallback is a $99-$149 add-on or a counsel-authored standard-plus-template bundle that competes on cost with DOTScreener.

competitors.name: Camus Energy and Ascend Analytics (utility forecasting and grid software)
competitors.what_they_do: Camus sells flexible-connection and grid-optimization software, and its CEO is the source of the '5 to 10 times more requests than builds' quote. competitors.name: NRECA Large Loads and Data Centers Learning Hub / Task Force
competitors.what_they_do: Free guidance, webinars and a peer task force for co-ops evaluating large loads. The page shows no downloadable developer-vetting checklist, screening tool or vendor list. It is the free-content substitute and also the natural distribution channel.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Trade association serving about 900 co-ops. Not a commercial competitor, but it can commoditize a '12 signs' checklist.

result.white_space:
I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.
result.evidence_of_demand:
The problem is documented and painful. Willingness to pay a third party for the fix is only partly evidenced. I found no RFPs for outsourced vetting and no vendor selling it.

Problem evidence:
- 5 to 10 times more requests than builds (Camus CEO Astrid Atkinson, in https://www.utilitydive.com/news/a-fraction-of-proposed-data-centers-will-get-built-utilities-are-wising-up/748214/). The same article cites an EPRI survey: among 10 utilities with data-center requests at 50% or more of peak load, none expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and about 30% of utilities derate loads based on maturity signals.
- Central Electric Power Cooperative (a G&T) says it has 'probably talked to over 100 developers', that some smaller prospects lack transparency, and that its lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers, up from 5-10% (https://cepci.org/the-rise-of-data-centers/).
- Tri-State has 10 large-load requests of 45-650 MW and wrote a High Impact Load tariff, which FERC rejected on jurisdiction (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/ferc-tri-state-large-load-tariff-data-center-doe/804076/).
- Coverage of shell-LLC and duplicate 'phantom' requests: https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/phantom-data-centers-are-flooding-the-load-queue/ and https://propmodo.com/utilities-call-bluff-on-speculative-data-center-load-demands/.

Cost pass-through evidence (supports the applicant-pays model):
- Great River Energy 'bills petitioners for the staff work related to vetting large-load requests so the cost doesn't fall on members' (Utility Dive link above).
- Central's data center customers pay the deposit and the initial study (cepci.org link above).

Counter-evidence:
- The Utility Dive article and https://rmi.org/resources/planners-have-tools-to-manage-large-load-forecast-uncertainty-are-they-working/ describe the responses as tariffs, collateral, derating and back-testing, not outsourced diligence.
- Large IOUs build this in-house, for example Georgia Power's Monte Carlo load-realization model.
- The NRECA hub offers free guidance but no vetting tool.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not sell it as a 12-point diligence memo shop, because tariffs and collateral will eat the easy checks. Sell it as the outsourced intake desk and shared duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT.

1. Wedge: partner with one G&T or state association that is already fielding many inquiries (Great River Energy, Tri-State, Central-style G&Ts). Back-test their last 10 inquiries for free, then run intake for them as a fixed-fee, applicant-paid service, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Utilities then buy it as a study-deposit line item, not a new budget item.
2. Moat: the pooled duplicate-request and LLC-principal graph across co-ops, states and utilities. Texas mandates duplicate disclosure only in ERCOT, and nobody runs one elsewhere. Every additional co-op makes it more valuable. Memos are the entry product and the registry is the business.
3. Lead with the checks an outsider can verify from public records: air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, deeds and options, LLC principals across states, water and stormwater filings, and cross-utility duplicates. Treat OEM slots and financing letters as applicant-supplied attestations to verify with a phone call, not as scraped data.
4. Integrate with GridUnity and PowerClerk as their pre-queue front door instead of competing. License or partner on Cleanview-style permit data rather than rebuilding it.
5. Fast test: a paid 'phantom back-test' for 3 co-ops. If they will not pay $7.5K for a live inquiry memo, the applicant-pays thesis is dead. Watch for engineering consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and others) adding this service line, which I could not rule out."

result.white_space:
Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed.
result.evidence_of_demand: Little verified. The only sourced item is background: Wikipedia states that a purchaser is usually entitled to a refund of the unused portion of GAP premium when the vehicle is sold or refinanced early (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gap_insurance). That supports the underlying entitlement but not spend or willingness to pay. I found no forum complaints, RFPs, or documents showing lender spend on this workaround. My recollection is that CFPB Supervisory Highlights and enforcement actions have cited auto servicers for failing to refund unearned add-on premiums, but I could not fetch or confirm it here (the CFPB URLs I tried returned 404). Treat that as a lead to check. Consumer-facing demand is described in the idea but not verified by URL.
result.kill_reason: n/a - no dominant incumbent or crowded set of direct competitors was found. Confidence is only low to moderate because search was unavailable. The idea's lender-side wedge is unconfirmed as unserved, and the repossession-deficiency side may overlap with lenders' in-house recovery.
result.sharper_angle:
Lead with the repossession-deficiency wedge and the compliance framing, not the payoff-desk success-fee play.

(1) Sell an attorney-ready deficiency and add-on-credit audit to consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense firms and legal aid. Buyers there have no in-house tooling, the incentives run in the borrower's favor, and statutory damages and fee-shifting under UCC Article 9 can fund the audit fee. Validate this first, since it needs no CU integration.

(2) For credit unions, reposition the payoff product as a flat-fee holder-liability control. It would be a retrospective audit quantifying unrefunded add-ons on paid-off loans, then a per-payoff automation with an audit trail that satisfies examiners. Do not take 20-30% from members' refunds.

(3) Start in one or two states with statutory automatic-refund rules, such as New Jersey. Build the administrator playbook there and use the data as the moat.

(4) Approach Origence or similar LOS vendors as a partner or acquirer early, before they build it as a feature.

Before committing, re-run the competitor and demand research with search restored. The checks: named consumer refund services, lender BPO vendors, F&I-cancellation tools from Reynolds, RouteOne and Dealertrack, and CFPB supervisory findings.

result.white_space:
The resale desk is not white space. SLS, ITRenew/Iron Mountain, SK tes and GreenTek already harvest and test DRAM, CPUs and GPUs, resell them, and offer revenue-share terms with serialized custody. Several are backed by public or strategic capital and have robotics and buyer networks.

The policy layer is only partly covered. NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (final Sept 26, 2025) already says volatile media 'fails to retain its contents after power is removed' and that organizations should focus sanitization on non-volatile media. It says purge can be more appropriate than destroy when reuse, resale, cost or lease returns matter, and that destruction blocks reuse by others. It also points to OEM Statements of Volatility. So the 'shred everything is a habit' insight is right. But the framework is public and a 10-page matrix is easy for any ITAD to copy. As a standalone $10-30K product it is weak.

What I found nobody offering:
(1) An independent, auditor-attested, per-model component persistence matrix mapped to regulator and CISO language (HIPAA, FFIEC/GLBA, PCI, SOX), with named sign-off and liability behind it. ITADs handle this client by client.
(2) Measured persistence for AI-server parts: GPU HBM and NVSwitch state, BlueField/ConnectX flash, BMC and firmware. Nobody appears to publish this the way DIMM volatility is documented.
(3) Per-serial, component-level custody evidence that a bank's auditor accepts without re-litigating policy each time.

Additional caveat: my searches were limited (see the evidence field), so a small startup doing (1) or (2) could exist unseen.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for component-level reuse and resale is real, and incumbents are already collecting the money:
- Iron Mountain's 10-K shows a large business selling decommissioned IT components, with buyers concentrated in China, and says it competes with hyperscalers' in-house programs: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1020569/000102056926000013/irm-20251231.htm. Its Q2 2026 10-Q reports ALM growth from new and existing customers and recent acquisitions: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1020569/000102056926000071/irm-20260630.htm
- Sumitomo invested in GreenTek in July 2026 explicitly because AI-driven data center buildouts shorten replacement cycles: https://www.sumitomocorp.com/en/jp/news/topics/2026/group/20260714
- SLS says 2022-23 AI GPU fleets are 'entering refresh cycles' and that the open market discounts what it cannot verify (https://www.simslifecycle.com/data-center/gpu/). It says millions of DDR4 modules have been redeployed (https://www.simslifecycle.com/data-center/hyperscale/).
- GreenTek buys B300/B200/H100 systems and memory today: https://www.greenteksolutionsllc.com/sell-used-it-equipment/ai-hardware-buyback
- SK tes advertises buyback, leaseback and revenue-share deals: https://www.sktes.com/it-services/data-center-decommissioning
- Microsoft reports a 92% reuse and recycling rate for cloud hardware: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/sustainability/circular-centers
- NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 supports reuse-friendly sanitization: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/final (PDF text: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf)
- TrendForce's press page shows a DRAM module revenue surge (+59% YoY in 2025): https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news. I did not verify the idea's '+400%' figure.

What I did not find: any evidence that banks or healthcare organizations still shred whole servers at scale, any complaint threads, RFPs, or a published price for a standalone sanitization-policy or sign-off product. I also could not verify the 'eight figures from pre-triage' claim. WebSearch was out of budget at the start of this task (200 of 200 already used). The work therefore used direct page fetches, SEC filings and NIST text only, with no forum, Crunchbase, Product Hunt or YC searches. result.sharper_angle:
Drop the resale desk and the revenue-share model. SLS, Iron Mountain/ITRenew, SK tes and GreenTek already run it with robotics, buyer networks and capital. Build only the missing trust layer, in this form:

(1) An independent 'Component Persistence and Disposition Standard'. It is a per-server-model, machine-readable matrix built from OEM Statements of Volatility and independent lab testing. It covers data-bearing parts (SSD/NVMe, NVDIMM, BMC, NIC/DPU flash, TPM) and, first, AI-server parts that the public documents cover poorly: GPU HBM and NVSwitch state, BlueField/ConnectX flash, and firmware.
(2) Map each component to NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 categories and to regulator and CISO policy language for banks and healthcare (HIPAA, FFIEC/GLBA, PCI, SOX). Deliver it as a signed policy addendum that a CISO and external auditor can adopt in one meeting, ideally with an insurer or professional-liability backstop that the incumbents' certifications do not provide.
(3) Monetize through subscription plus per-serial attestation, not resale share. Sell it to regulated enterprises' GRC and IT asset teams and to neocloud finance and procurement. License it white-label to mid-size ITADs that lack the credibility or R&D to publish it. That turns Iron Mountain, SLS and GreenTek from competitors into channels or later acquirers, instead of fighting them for inventory.

Validate first with 5 to 10 CISOs or GRC leads in banks and health systems who currently mandate whole-server shredding. Ask whether they would pay $25-50K a year or per-rack fees for an attested policy. If none will, the idea has no independent business and should be dropped."

result.sharper_angle: Lead with the records and legal-standing wedge and stay asset-light. Sell a per-job 'stranded-job rescue file' to lenders, servicers and ABS trustees: recovered permit, interconnection and design records, a contractor-of-record transfer, a re-stamped design set, and a cure-cost and PTO-date estimate per tier. result.white_space: Descriptive tracking of redemption requests, caps, fill rates, runway and alerts is already covered, some of it free (Sekond's free tier, Trading Market Signals, Yardeni), so the tracker and paywalled alerts as pitched are not defensible. Nothing I found covers these pieces, and each is still open. (1) A forward-looking fill-rate forecast. Sekond's runway is a supply-side cash metric, Trading Market Signals' exit clock extrapolates the last fill rate, and Stanger and Blue Vault report history. Nobody publishes a next-window forecast with a timestamped track record. (2) A shadow NAV against reported NAV. Only commentary exists (Mercer Capital, LSEG, Octus, Blue Vault), plus Cox Capital's secondary bids as an implicit haircut; no product sells a per-fund adjusted NAV. (3) A decision tool for the choice advisers face now: wait through proration, or sell into a discounted mini-tender. Cox Capital has open offers at 12.5% to 35% below NAV on BCRED, HLEND, ADS, ASIF, OCIC and OTIC. I found no tool that puts expected fill, time to exit and the discount side by side. (4) Client-book-level output: per-client liquidity ladders, what to file, and compliance-file letters or memos tied to SEC exam and Reg BI liquidity-disclosure priorities. Sekond surfaces 'documents for redemption processing' but I found no client-letter or due-diligence-memo product. Cautions: the non-obvious insight (advisers over-request to offset expected proration) is already published by BofA and Khan Capital, so it is not proprietary. Binary gate probability is also low-information in this regime, because almost every large fund with requests above 10% gates at 5%; the value is in fill rate and time to exit. The category is cyclical, so the product has to extend to all evergreen wrappers (PE, real estate, infrastructure) to survive a calmer tape.
result.evidence_of_demand: Real but thinner than the idea assumes, and mostly for free products. (a) The pain is documented. PitchBook reports advisers 'must rely solely on periodic communications from fund managers' and are looking for independent information (https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/private-debt-liquidity-education-wealth-advisers). Sekond's launch coverage says the same (https://www.investmentnews.com/alternatives/fintech-startup-sekond-wants-to-bolster-advisors-private-markets-arsenal-with-liquidity-monitoring-tool/265980). (b) The stress is confirmed. BCRED gated at 5% in June 2026 after requests above 10% (https://www.readthedrift.com/blackstone-bcred-redemptions-explained/). Stanger recorded Q2 non-traded BDC requests at a record 12.4% of NAV with 38% filled (https://www.privatedebtinvestor.com/non-listed-bdc-fundraising-momentum-slowing-redemption-requests-rising-stanger/). BCRED capped again in Q3 with requests near 10% (https://altswire.com/bcred-caps-q3-repurchases-at-5-as-requests-hit-4-3b-about-10-of-shares/). Blue Owl's OCIC and OTIC saw requests of 22% and 41% (https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/blue-owl-holds-bdc-withdrawals-at-5-after-redemption-requests-of-41-22). (c) Regulation is pushing spend on this. The SEC's FY2026 exam priorities stress liquidity, valuation and disclosure of illiquid products, and FINRA and Reg BI require due diligence and liquidity-risk disclosure for non-traded BDCs (https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-132-sec-division-examinations-announces-2026-priorities). (d) Existing spend and price points. Sekond lists $499/mo per user and $20K/yr enterprise (https://sekond.co/pricing) and claims 50 wealth teams and 15 sponsors, though most use the free tier. Blue Vault sells subscriptions to broker-dealers and RIAs (https://bluevaultpartners.com/who-we-are/nontraded-bdc-research/). Interval Fund Tracker charges $450 per year (https://intervalfundtracker.com/register/tender-offer-basic/). Mini-tender bidders such as Cox Capital price off listed-BDC discounts (https://altswire.com/cox-capital-launches-discounted-tender-offers-for-bcred-hlend-shares/), which shows demand for a shadow-NAV view. Missing evidence: I found no proof that RIAs pay $400 to $1,500 per month for redemption analytics. The cheapest legacy data is $450 per year and the good free tools are already out there.
result.sharper_angle: Drop the tracker and the alert paywall, since Sekond, Trading Market Signals and Yardeni give that away. Build only the decision layer nobody has: a fill-rate and time-to-exit forecast plus shadow NAV, wrapped in a 'wait, tender, or sell into a mini-tender' calculator run against the adviser's actual client book. Ingest holdings from Addepar, Orion or custodian feeds. For each client, show expected fill this window, cumulative liquidity over the next 4 to 6 windows, and the expected-value comparison against live secondary bids (Cox Capital offers at 12.5% to 35% below NAV, which expire and so create urgency). Auto-generate the compliance-file letter and Reg BI liquidity-disclosure memo for each recommendation. Publish every forecast with a timestamp and score it each quarter to build a public track record, which no competitor has. Sell to RIA compliance heads and CIOs at $500 to $1,500 per month, and license the forecast API to Addepar, Orion, iCapital and CAIS, or to Sekond, instead of competing with their trackers. Widen to all evergreen wrappers so it survives a calmer market. Before building, run a two-week test: publish next-window fill-rate forecasts for about 15 funds ahead of Q4 tender results and check accuracy, then see whether 10 RIAs will pay $500 per month for the client-level output over Sekond's free tier.

GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. (c) Dividend Finance says it defers payments and helps find replacement installers where feasible (https://news.bloomberglaw.com/bankruptcy-law/solar-panel-bankruptcies-leave-frustrated-homeowners-in-limbo). result.white_space:
Research limits: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran no searches. I used direct fetches of known URLs (Wikipedia, Cornell LII for the UCC text, SunStrong, Sunnova, Qualia, TitleCapture, Simplifile, the YC directory) and a GitHub repo search. Several guessed URLs 404'd or returned 403. Competitor coverage is therefore thin, and I found no funded startup doing solar-specific lien-lapse analysis and curative for title agents. Absence in my results is weak evidence, not proof.

Unserved as far as I could tell: a title-agent-facing, per-file workflow that (a) classifies the instrument (UCC-1 fixture filing vs. SOS-only filing vs. recorded memorandum or notice of lease vs. PACE vs. mortgage), (b) computes lapse under UCC 9-515, and (c) routes the file to the current servicer with a pre-formatted payoff, estoppel or UCC-3 request. Incumbent UCC vendors and general title-clearing outsourcers do not appear to package this for solar.

Substantive weaknesses to weigh against the gap:
- Lapse is not death. Cornell LII (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-515) confirms that on lapse the interest becomes unperfected, and is deemed never perfected only as against a purchaser for value. The debt and the interest against the debtor survive. In a lease or PPA the lessor owns the equipment, so a lapse memo does not clear ownership or the lease. The buyer still needs an assumption or buyout. Underwriters may therefore refuse to rely on 'lapsed, no exception' memos, and getting one to accept a format is the make-or-break step.
- Debtor-filed terminations are narrow. UCC 9-509(d)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-509) requires the secured party to have failed to comply with 9-513, plus debtor authorization and a statement on the form. That generally means a demand and a wait, and it only works where no obligation is still secured. That conflicts with a 48-hour SLA.
- The 'orphan' premise is overstated for Sunnova, the biggest name. Its assets went to new owners and SunStrong runs a home-sale transfer process. The truly orphaned pool (Mosaic, PosiGen, small defunct installers) is smaller and messier. Sunnova is confirmed only via Wikipedia and the SunStrong and Sunnova sites. I could not fetch a Mosaic or PosiGen page.
- Unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure for underwriter-facing lapse opinions unless an attorney of record signs.
- Per-county recording quirks make it operations-heavy, not pure software.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Weak and mostly indirect. I found no forum threads, RFPs, or published spend figures because search was unavailable, and Reddit is blocked to WebFetch.

What I could confirm:
- Title insurers require curative steps such as releases before issuing clean policies, and otherwise except the item (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_insurance). This confirms the general workflow exists and is paid for.
- The solar wave is real. Sunnova filed Chapter 11 on June 9, 2025 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunnova).
- Sunnova customers have a live successor with a home-sale transfer process (https://sunstrongmanagement.com), which shows sale-time transfers are a recognized friction point.
- The SunStrong page has no title-agent or UCC-3 guidance, so agents are pointed at a customer-service form. That leaves a real service gap and is the best demand signal I found.

Not found and not verifiable this session: customer complaints about solar UCC liens blocking closings, title-agent willingness to pay $395-$900 per file, or any underwriter bulletin accepting lapse memos. The 'consumer SEO sites serve this' claim in the idea is also unconfirmed.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not sell 'lien autopsy as a service' with a lapse memo as the product. It rests on a legally soft claim (lapse is not extinguishment, and leases and PPAs survive it). Instead build a solar-exception resolver for title agents and underwriters:

1. Classify every solar item found in a title search (UCC-1 fixture filing, SOS-only filing, recorded notice or memorandum of lease, PACE, loan vs. lease vs. PPA) and give the correct resolution path for each. Lapse is one branch, alongside payoff, buyer assumption or buyout, and subordination.
2. Keep a living directory of current holders and servicers (SunStrong for the Sunnova book, Sunrun, Tesla, Mosaic and PosiGen successors, etc.), with each one's actual transfer, payoff and UCC-3 contact and turnaround.
3. Auto-generate the request packets (payoff or estoppel request, 9-513 authenticated demand, UCC-3, county-format cover sheets) and chase them with tracking.
4. Get one title underwriter to pre-approve the decision tree and memo format, and have a licensed attorney of record countersign to avoid the unauthorized-practice-of-law problem.

Distribution and pricing: sell to underwriters and agency groups first, since they carry the claims risk and feel the pain of exceptions, and integrate with Qualia or SoftPro. Price per resolved exception, with a subscription for the servicer directory and tracking, rather than a per-file contingency on unpredictable outcomes. A later, stronger wedge is selling the transfer-request intake to the servicers themselves (SunStrong and the other post-bankruptcy servicers), who are absorbing thousands of home-sale requests through a customer-service form. Before building, validate demand with 10 to 15 title-agent and underwriter interviews, and run a real search pass for competitors, because this session's research was budget-limited.

result.white_space:
Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Moderate. The service is proven and paid for, but I found no direct evidence that solo attorneys pay for tooling.

- Paying customers for the lawsuit itself: Bertollini charges a $5,000 flat fee plus $500 court costs (https://www.mandamus.com). It also runs a dense funnel of pages per form type and district, which implies steady inbound demand: https://www.mandamus.com/uscis-mandamus-by-district.html
- Government behaviour that supports the core insight: 'USCIS often reaches out within 45 days to propose a consent order, or simply resumes processing within weeks of being served'; 45-90 day resolutions are common (https://www.mandamus.com). Voluntary dismissal after agency action runs at 83-85% in EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI, and 68-70% in SDTX and D.D.C. (https://www.mandamus.com/uscis-mandamus-by-district.html). These come from one attorney's self-reported analysis, not an independent dataset.
- Structural demand drivers: the October 2025 end of the 540-day automatic EAD extension made I-765 mandamus a 'primary remedy' (https://www.mandamus.com/case-law-updates.html). Thirteen D.D.C. delay decisions in ten weeks show ongoing volume (https://www.mandamus.com/mandamus-decisions-summer-2026.html).
- DIY appetite: a free pro se guide with templates exists and describes 'high procedural risk' from service, venue and naming errors, which is the pain point the idea targets (https://www.mandamus.com/pro-se-mandamus-guide.html).
- Volume signal is mixed. CourtListener/RECAP is a crowdsourced subset, so treat these counts as directional only. Search 'Citizenship and Immigration Services' + mandamus + delay, by filing year: 2023 = 385, 2024 = 352, 2025 = 477, 2026 to date = 221. There is no visible 2026 surge in that sample, and the 'decade-high' claim in the pitch is unverified. Source: https://www.courtlistener.com/api/rest/v4/search/?q=%22Citizenship+and+Immigration+Services%22+mandamus+delay&type=r&filed_after=2025-01-01&filed_before=2025-12-31
- Not found: any RFP, forum thread or survey showing solo lawyers paying $350-600 per filing for a tool. Reddit was blocked from fetching, and no searches were possible.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop 'delay-suit rails for everything' and become the outcome-intelligence and triage layer for routine delay suits, sold through the software solos already use.

1. Lead with the data, not the drafting. Build a district x form-type x judge database of filing-to-adjudication time, voluntary-dismissal rate, motion-to-dismiss grant rate, and consent-order versus quiet-adjudication outcomes. Source it from CourtListener/RECAP and PACER, and publish freely a 'will this get mooted in this district' score. Mandamus.com already publishes 7 districts of this by hand, so the defensible version is broader (all 94 districts), refreshed, judge-level and machine-readable, with the private layer being attorneys' own logged results.
2. Sell a narrow pack, not a general platform. Cover only routine delays where the moot-by-adjudication pattern is strongest: post-interview N-400, I-751, I-90, I-765 EAD renewals (the post-October-2025 primary remedy) and long-idle I-130/I-140, filed in the high-moot districts (EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ, EDMI and similar). Explicitly exclude or flag the weak cases, namely nationality-hold suits (D.D.C. dismisses on TRAC) and I-485 in the Fifth Circuit (Cheejati). Replace S.D. Tex. with a friendlier launch district.
3. Build in the fee logic. Include a consent-order-first settlement template and an EAJA/Buckhannon checklist, so the firm's flat fee stays profitable and any fee claim is preserved.
4. Distribute via the incumbent rather than against it. Ship as a Docketwise-integrated add-on, or a 'stuck case' triage widget inside case-management tools, since Docketwise has no litigation feature and already sits on the receipt dates and form types.
5. Treat boutique mandamus firms as customers and channel partners, not enemies. Sell them the analytics and overflow-filing capacity, and be careful with any referral economics because of fee-splitting rules.

Validate first with real searches (the ones this research could not run) and with 10 concierge filings that log outcomes. The go/no-go signal is whether 5 solos will pay $400 per filing when a free guide and a $5,000 boutique already exist."

Research limits: the WebSearch budget ran out (200/200) before any search, so I could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, forums or RFPs. This verdict rests on direct fetches of incumbent sites and background knowledge, and confidence is medium-low. Many sites returned 503/403 or thin homepages.

What I found. The physical model (bins, scheduled pickup, chip and fluid recovery, weigh systems, aggregating into loads for mills) is what Sims, Cohen and OmniSource already do as their core business. Specialty Ti/Ni alloy dealers already buy segregated turnings from aerospace shops at grade-based prices. I found no funded startup that combines all of these: RFID two-bin alloy segregation, an XRF-plus-scale route truck, a shared ledger across many small shops, and a digital chain-of-custody certificate. But I could not search Crunchbase or YC to rule one out.

1. Independent transparency for the 20-300 employee shop. Incumbents make money on the information gap (the 'you left $X in your bin' claim). A neutral assayer who shows the shop what its bin is worth, and who does not own the truck or the mill relationship, is a conflict the dealers cannot copy.
2. Prime and OEM revert or closed-loop chain-of-custody for tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers. I found no evidence of a productized, cross-dealer certificate for small shops. This is the only part of the idea that looks genuinely unserved.
3. Small-shop Ti/Inconel/Hastelloy streams where the shop can't get mill-direct pricing.

Weak parts. The claim that shops 'never see' their bin value is probably overstated for titanium and nickel alloys, where dealers already assay and pay premiums, so the mixed-lot penalty falls mostly on stainless, brass and tool-steel shops. The trucking, briquetting and coolant-recovery arms are capex-heavy and put a startup in head-on competition with incumbents that have 230+ yards. The revenue math ($1,500/month chip value per shop, 60 shops, 20-30% spread) yields a thin, working-capital-heavy hauling business. Incumbents can copy the 'transparency statement' cheaply, and I could not verify the Section 232 'US-melted content' premium (the CBP page returned 404).

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

result.sharper_angle:
Do not build a marketplace that buys parts from every plumber. Build a neutral evidence custodian embedded in channels where the claim number and the payer are already known at dispatch.

1. Start with insurer-dispatched and insurer-funded plumber programs (emergency plumbing and leak-response networks, preferred-vendor programs, home-warranty and service-plan networks). The insurer controls the vendor, so the bounty and bag become a contracted line item in the dispatch workflow. There is no cold-start recruiting of independent shops and no orphaned parts with no claim.
2. Limit the wedge to 4-5 part types where product-defect subrogation is strongest and the part is small and cheap to ship: braided supply lines, ice-maker lines, toilet connectors, PEX fittings, water heater components.
3. Position as a neutral, joint-exam-ready custodian (documented protocol, notice to all interested parties, photo and QR chain of custody, homeowner e-sign). Insurers get admissible evidence, and manufacturers cannot easily cite spoliation. Do not sell a cause-of-loss opinion. Provide factual photo records and route to licensed engineers, or partner with one such as Donan-type firms as the escalation path.
4. Sell first to subrogation vendors and recovery law firms that work on contingency and need the part before they take a $10k file. Their willingness to advance $75-150 per part is the fastest demand test.
5. Keep the failure dataset private and consortium-style for participating insurers, with anonymized aggregate reporting by product line and date code. Skip a public Backblaze-style brand naming until there is enough volume and legal review. License to manufacturers only after that.
6. Before building, run the cheap kill test: hand-collect 50 parts, take 20 case files to two mutual insurers and one subrogation vendor, and get a written 'we would have pursued these' count and a per-part price. Also finish the missing searches (Crunchbase, YC, trade press) that this run could not do.

result.white_space:
Narrow, and mostly not in what the idea sells. Form generation and e-filing are commoditized. TaxBandits lists $0.80-$2.75/form, 1095EZ $3/form with a $750 minimum, and the IRIS portal is free for small filers. The idea's $1,500 minimum and $2-4 per form sit above the market. Loan-tape ingestion, VIN check digit, NHTSA plant lookup and an exception report are already claimed by Morado, which also targets credit unions with core-file ingestion. What looks unserved:
- Fixing the data. Lenders whose loan systems lack a VIN, or have bad ones, need them recovered from titles, lien records and dealer contract packets, with borrower and dealer outreach tracked. Nobody visibly sells this as a managed service.
- Mixed-purpose SPVL allocation, meaning GAP, warranty and other add-ons financed in the loan, plus refinance and loan-acquisition edge cases.
- Original-use and new-versus-used determination for indirect paper, plus a defensible per-loan evidence record for 6721/6722 penalty defense.
- Selling any of the above white-label to e-file vendors, CUSOs and core-adjacent vendors that lack VIN features (TaxBandits, Tax1099), not per form to small lenders.
The market is small even where it is unserved. Only new, U.S.-assembled, personal-use vehicles qualify, so buy-here-pay-here and used-car lenders will have few or no reportable loans. The deduction runs only 2025-2028, so there are at most about three filing seasons (2026, 2027 and 2028 tax years).
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for compliance is real and mandated. Willingness to pay is already being captured at low prices.
- Final regulations (TD 10054, 91 FR 57214, published 2026-09-08, effective 2026-11-09) require reporting on specified passenger vehicle loans of $600 or more of interest. Treasury acknowledged that commenters, including credit unions, said lenders lack the data. It said lenders 'may need to collect additional information', declined safe harbors and declined substitute or summary statements. This confirms the idea's premise. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/08/2026-18219/car-loan-interest-deduction (I read the text; the preamble also approves NHTSA VIN-lookup reliance.)
- Paid products already exist and are priced: TaxBandits https://www.taxbandits.com/1099-forms/efile-form-1098-vli/ ($0.80-$2.75/form), 1095EZ https://www.vehicleloaninterest.com/ ($3-$4.50/form, $750 minimum), Tax1099 https://www.tax1099.com/1098-forms/efile-form-1098-vli, and Morado https://morado1099.com/industries/credit-unions. Vendors do not build 1098-VLI products without expected buyers.
- Morado's guide says America's Credit Unions filed comment letters on the proposed regulations asking for lender safe harbors. It also calls the VIN/original-use/final-assembly data capture the hardest lender problem: https://www.morado1099.com/resources/irs-form-1098-vli-guide
- CU Today ran 'IRS Releases Final Form For New Car Loan Interest Deduction' on 2026-09-28; I found it only as a Google News listing, not the article, so it is a weak signal.
- I found no RFPs, forum complaints or spend data showing that lenders will pay a premium for VIN cleansing beyond the e-file price. I could not verify any core-processor plans. The WebSearch budget ran out and Bing scraping was inconsistent, so coverage of niche vendors and trade-group content is incomplete.
result.kill_reason: Crowded with no credible white space for the idea as written. At least four live direct competitors sell the same loan-tape-to-1098-VLI-to-IRIS flow. Morado already advertises the differentiators (VIN check digit, NHTSA U.S.-assembly lookup, GVWR, SPVL allocation, per-loan exception preflight) and targets credit unions and CUSOs with core-file ingestion. Filing is priced at $0.80-$3/form, or free via the IRS portal for small filers, against the proposed $2-4 with a $1,500 minimum. The plant-table moat is undercut by the free NHTSA vPIC API and Treasury's explicit approval of the NHTSA lookup. Buy-here-pay-here and used-car lenders will report little because only new, U.S.-assembled vehicles qualify. The deduction sunsets after 2028. Core processors could bundle the form output, though I found no announcement.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not build a per-form 1098-VLI filing service for small lenders. If any version is worth pursuing, make it a narrow B2B2B data-remediation layer that sits upstream of existing filers:
1. Sell an API or managed service that fixes VIN and collateral gaps and returns a per-loan evidence record. The record would cover recovered VIN, original-use basis, final-assembly source (plant code or label), and SPVL allocation for financed add-ons, plus refinance and acquisition handling.
2. Sell it white-label to TaxBandits-style e-file vendors, CUSOs and indirect-lending platforms, which lack VIN features, rather than to individual credit unions.
3. Lead with a paid readiness audit on a 500-loan tape, priced as a fixed fee rather than per form.
Treat it as a one-season, roughly three-year-sunset revenue opportunity, not a venture-scale company. Before building, run the free-audit test from the first 30 days. Check whether more than a handful of lenders actually have VIN gaps that Morado's preflight would not already flag, and whether lenders pay to close them rather than just fail loans out of the file.

result.white_space: The market is not empty: TrueLoad already sells software-only NEC 220.87 reports from utility interval data to heat pump and EV installers at $30/project, and the underlying calc is even open-source. The white space is what TrueLoad says it does not do, plus the liability-bearing layer nobody has bundled. (1) A stamped, licensed-professional deliverable. Small HVAC and EV contractors without in-house electricians must take on risk when they self-certify a software report, and WattMonk shows they pay for stamped desk work in solar. (2) Photo-of-panel intake, so installers do not hand-key service details. (3) A cheapest-path recommendation with a compliant load-management spec and bill of materials (NEC 625.42 EVEMS, 750 energy management, 705.13 power control systems), which TrueLoad explicitly lacks and hardware vendors only offer for their own products. (4) Doing the utility interval-data retrieval for the contractor, which is the real friction, since TrueLoad's own guides tell users to request it themselves. (5) HVAC and heat-pump contractors as the buyer, with a pre-check integrated into state or utility programs. Weak points: a $79-149 price against a $30 software anchor needs the stamp and outcome to justify a 3-5x premium; solar desks like WattMonk or Aurora can add this as a SKU; and I could not verify Qmerit or unknown small engineering shops.
result.evidence_of_demand: Thin and mostly indirect. My WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run forum, Reddit or RFP searches, so demand research is limited to direct page fetches and GitHub code search. No direct evidence found of contractors paying for stamped load-calc desk work in electrification; the closest is WattMonk's outsourced solar permit and PE-stamp model. Indirect signals: (a) SPAN's marketing claims panel-upgrade avoidance saves homeowners $3-20K and 3-9 months (https://www.span.io). (b) Emporia sells a whole EV-charger line on 'no panel upgrade' load management (https://www.emporiaenergy.com). (c) WattMonk reports 400+ installers and 125,000+ projects, so installers do outsource engineering desk work (https://www.wattmonk.com). (d) Aurora sells 24-48 hour plan sets to 7,000+ organizations (https://aurorasolar.com). (e) PermitFlow's $54M Series B shows contractor permit workflow is funded (https://www.permitflow.com). (f) DOE says the IRA HEEHR rebates can fund 'electric wiring and load service center upgrades' (https://www.energy.gov/scep/home-energy-rebates-programs), but the federal 25C credit for panel upgrades expired for property placed in service after Dec 31, 2025 (https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/energy-efficient-home-improvement-credit), so this tailwind has weakened. (g) At least two tiny startups or side projects (TrueLoad, TradesQuote) built products and SEO content around 'do I need a panel upgrade' and NEC 220.87, and TrueLoad claims AHJs 'increasingly want a formal calculation' (https://trueloadapp.com/resources/). That is a self-reported and weak signal. The idea's own labor-shortage figures (electrician shortage, 2-month delays) were not independently verified.
result.sharper_angle: Do not sell 'a load calculation'. TrueLoad sells that at $30, PanelWright gives it away, and hardware vendors give design support for free. Sell an insured, stamped 'panel-upgrade-avoidance package' per job. It has four parts. (1) Do the utility interval-data pull for the contractor (Green Button/AMI, or ship a 30-day logger where AMI is missing) instead of asking them to request it. (2) Deliver the stamped NEC 220.87 report. (3) Add a stamped load-management design: a vendor-neutral device recommendation, the NEC 625.42/750/705.13 basis and the bill of materials. (4) Add an AHJ-acceptance layer. Launch in one or two states with AMI-heavy utilities and heat-pump incentives, pre-clear the local AHJs, and go to market through heat-pump distributors, utility or state programs and OEM channels rather than 20 cold-sold contractors. Use outcome-based pricing, such as a low base fee plus a success fee or a subscription only when the upgrade is avoided, to justify the premium over $30 software. Fix a technical flaw in the current pitch: 220.87 needs recorded peak demand (12 months of interval or demand data, or a 30-day recording), so a photo plus monthly utility bills will not suffice. Also verify Qmerit and the solar engineering desks before committing, since WattMonk or Aurora could ship this SKU quickly. Treat TrueLoad as a possible partner or acquisition target rather than only a competitor.

result.white_space: Limited to what I could check: I found no vendor, on the pages I fetched, that runs a managed, longitudinal panel of verified GLP-1 users segmented by drug, dose and weeks on therapy. I also found none that does physical product testing on that panel (sensory, portion and format tests, home-use tests) or maps aversions by texture and smell against dose. The players found are all survey, signal or purchase-data based: Circana and Numerator show what GLP-1 households buy, Hartman sells a one-off $10k survey report, and Tastewise sells AI trend signals. Nothing found covers household spillover modeling tied to a panel. Nothing found offers claim-substantiation studies (8-12 week muscle and satiety) for 'GLP-1 friendly' labels. Big gaps in my evidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not run general web searches and relied on direct fetches of vendor pages. I did not check startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, sensory CROs (Sensory Spectrum showed no GLP-1 content; Tragon and Eurofins fetches failed), generic panel vendors (Cint, Toluna showed no GLP-1 content; Dynata unchecked), telehealth companies (Ro, Noom, WeightWatchers) that could monetize their own user bases, or flavor houses (Givaudan, Kerry and dsm-firmenich showed no GLP-1 content on the pages retrieved; IFF returned 403). Any of these could already offer a GLP-1 screener or a similar service, so treat the gap verdict as medium-low confidence.
result.evidence_of_demand: Real, paid spend on GLP-1 consumer intelligence exists, but it is on a different deliverable. (1) Hartman Group sells a $10,000 GLP-1 report with a 1,103-user oversample, so CPG insights teams pay five figures for GLP-1 user data: https://www.hartman-group.com/reports/272892157/glp-1s-seizing-opportunity-in-a-new-cpg-landscape. (2) Circana reports 23% of US households use GLP-1s and projects users at 35% of F&B units by 2030, which shows the market is large and the data vendors have made it a marquee topic: https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 (published 18 Nov 2025). Circana notes GLP-1 users still outspend non-users overall. (3) Numerator has productized 'GLP-1 People Groups' and 'GLP-1 Custom Analysis' and published a restaurant GLP-1 report, showing incumbents are investing in the segment: https://www.numerator.com/glp-1/. (4) Tastewise reports that Conagra, Nestle (Vital Pursuit) and Smoothie King have launched GLP-1-targeted lines, and the page cites 82.8% of GLP-1 users prioritizing protein (page stats are unattributed): https://tastewise.io/report/glp-1-us. That supports the claim that CPG is mid-reformulation and needs tests. Not found: any RFP, forum complaint or budget line showing that R&D teams want or pay for GLP-1 sensory or home-use testing panels or claim-substantiation studies. The idea's stats (73% taste change, 70% lose joy in eating, $25-150k per study) are unverified here. Demand for GLP-1 insight is proven at about $10k per report, and demand at $25-150k per study is not proven.
result.sharper_angle: Do not start as a general 'GLP-1 panel', because Hartman, Circana and Numerator already own GLP-1 survey insights and can add a screener. Start with a tighter, harder-to-copy wedge: a longitudinal, dose- and week-on-therapy-tagged aversion panel for physical products, sold first to protein, frozen and foodservice (hospital and senior-living) R&D teams. The first product is fast, cheap sensory and portion tests that mail samples to verified users and return aversion maps by texture and smell, priced as a $40-100k/year subscription with pay-per-test add-ons. Recruit through GLP-1 dietitian and telehealth partners, so dose and duration are verified by a provider and not self-reported from Reddit. That solves both credibility and privacy or health-data risk. Treat the 8-12 week claim-substantiation studies as a later phase delivered with a CRO partner and IRB oversight, since they are a clinical business and not a panel business. Position against survey vendors as 'what they will actually eat at dose X, week Y', which purchase panels and surveys cannot produce. Before building, do the checks I could not: search for sensory CROs and panel vendors already selling GLP-1 audiences, YC and Crunchbase entries, and telehealth companies that could offer the same panel themselves.
